text:
[FISM](https://chbrown.github.io/kdd-2013-usb/kdd/p659.pdf) is a direct precedent for candidate-to-history scoring: aggregate learned item–item similarities over the user’s history, with history-length normalization. [Fossil](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.09152) adds a weighted sum over recent items, using global and user-specific weights for each sequence lag. These are learned collaborative similarities; Fossil’s temporal weighting concerns sequence position, not elapsed-time decay. Both aggregate evidence additively, without explicitly requiring two supporting historical items.

[NAIS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.07053) provides a closer precedent for candidate-dependent history weighting: attention learns which historical items matter for each target. [FBSM](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.11799) supplies the content-based connection, learning bilinear similarities between candidate features and previously preferred items. Its feature interactions concern combinations of item features; they do not establish corroboration by two distinct historical items. These precedents support similarity aggregation and adaptive weighting, but do not establish novelty or effectiveness of a two-witness rule.

Proposed controls: freeze identical title/description representations and candidate–history similarities, then compare maximum similarity, normalized sum, recency-weighted sum, top-two mean, and second-largest similarity. Maximum pooling permits one strong match; second-largest similarity requires two distinct history items to score highly. Top-two mean can still be dominated by its strongest match. Compare each pooling rule with and without identical temporal weights, and remove the strongest matching history item to measure dependence on one witness. Deduplicate history item IDs before selecting witnesses. Keep the SASRec backbone, fusion tuning budget, candidate sets and validation users fixed; select by macro validation HR@10 across all four categories. These are proposed ablations, not reported findings.
